entries.title: The Bombmaker Next Door
entries.summary: "Last year, police found 400 bombs and booby traps in a dead man's home. 200 households were evacuated. So why did his neighbours adore him?"
entries.content:
When John Nelson died in the summer of 2025, he left behind more than 400 explosive devices, a literal minefield that ran through his home in the suburbs between Manchester and Liverpool. (“Minefield” may be misleading; there were also secret pits filled with spikes.) The painstaking work of clearing Nelson’s home of explosives prompted “one of the largest domestic evacuations of its kind in recent British history,” writes Andrew Kersley, who spent months interviewing the experts who kept Nelson’s home from exploding, as well as the neighbors who seemingly loved him. “I guess it was just his pastime,” one tells Kersley. Indeed!

During a second search after Nelson’s death, police had discovered a small tobacco tin containing explosives, with wires protruding from it. RY set up his X-ray machine and stepped into the adjoining room while it scanned the tin. As he reached for the door, he almost triggered the first booby trap: a fishing line wrapped around the handle that was attached to a rigged shotgun cartridge. Suddenly the contents of the house looked rather different. If one door had been trapped, any of them might be. So might any of the shoulder-high piles surrounding him.

More stories about neighbors

How I Became the Villain of El Cerrito’s Nextdoor

“I had a panic attack. Then I wrote an apology letter.”

What I Found When I Tried to Walk Across Dallas in a Day

“Determined to find adventure in my own backyard, I tramped across my famously pedestrian-averse hometown. The most memorable part turned out to be the serendipitous encounters with neighbors I met along the way.”

The Coyotes in the HOA

“Maybe we are the coyotes. We’ve invaded those tidy realms of whiteness, and we did not duck our heads. We acted like we owned the place.”

entries.title: Nothing but Highlights: Is Power Slap the Sport We Deserve?
entries.summary: "Slap fighting is the world’s newest combat sport. Built for short attention spans and super-viral moments, it’s aiming for global dominance."
entries.content:
Slapping someone in the face is now a sport. Yes, I’m surprised too. But in an era of ever-shrinking attention spans, getting to the point (or the slap) within seconds seems to be the surest way to hold viewers. According to its founder, Dana White, “Power Slap has secured more sponsorship revenue in its first two years than UFC did in its first decade.” Stuart McGurk deftly guides us through the rise of the slap, and talks with those who fear the consequences of hitting someone round the head as hard as you can.

The rules are straightforward. Competitors stand either side of a central podium. In each round, they are permitted to strike their opponent – open-handed, ungloved, cheek only – a single time. After one minute of recovery time, they must allow themselves to be struck back. Bouts range between three and five rounds. Victory can be earned on points – the three judges look for clean technique and the impact a strike makes – but about half are won via knockout. The podium is padded, as the competitors sometimes collide with it on the way down. Behind each competitor stand two catchers to grab them as they fall. When Power Slap introduced a super-heavyweight division, where contestants can weigh the same as an upright piano, they hired professional strongmen for the job.

More picks on violent sports

I Went to the White House Brawl and Watched the Manosphere Go Limp

“It was supposed to be an exhibition of freedom without restraint: a bombastic birthday boy, fourteen uncontrollable athletes, and a South Lawn build-out that was piss-your-pants patriotic. But what united onlookers, in the end, was the sudden realization that American machismo had hit a hard limit.”

Name of the Father

“A wiseguy’s son steps out of his father’s shadow—and into the boxing ring. But the legacy of organized crime isn’t so easy to leave behind.”

Boxer Patricio Manuel, a Transgender Pioneer, Is Still Looking for His Next Fight

“Manuel sees sports as the latest front in a culture war that fought — and lost — previous battles over same-sex marriage and trans bathroom bills.”

entries.title: Vegetabilities: A Harvest of a Reading List on Vegetables
entries.summary: Remarkable stories of our old reliables. Eat your veggies, kids!
entries.content:
Thoughtful stories for thoughtless times.

Longreads has published hundreds of original stories—personal essays, reported features, reading lists, and more—and more than 14,000 editor’s picks. And they’re all funded by readers like you. Become a member today.

Whenever I clean spinach or other greens, I get a curious feeling. I see a post-apocalyptic future, where a white-haired version of me is cleaning greens amid the ruins, salvaging every tiny, edible leaf. I then imagine my ancestors doing the same thing a hundred thousand years ago. Nothing heroic about this work, no high drama, no awesome mammoth-hunting. Just the fundamental stuff that keeps life going.

“In the temperate and tropical regions where it appears that hominids evolved into human beings, the principal food of the species was vegetable,” Ursula K. Le Guin reminds us in her classic The Carrier Bag Theory of Fiction. “Sixty-five to eighty percent of what human beings ate in those regions in Paleolithic, Neolithic, and prehistoric times was gathered; only in the extreme Arctic was meat the staple food.” 

Vegetables have quietly sustained us, season after season, year after year, for millennia. Down-to-earth and seemingly mundane, they claim deep love and reverence from those who care to look. Over time, we have even come to imbue vegetables with drama, heroes, stories. Are they (and we) made better by the act? Or do they only require simple, loving attention?

When Edward Espe Brown, Zen monk and chef, was a young student at the Tassajara Zen Mountain Center in California, he asked his teacher, Shunryū Suzuki Rōshi, for advice on working in the kitchen. “When you wash the rice,” Rōshi told him, “wash the rice. When you cut the carrots, cut the carrots. When you stir the soup, stir the soup.” 

It takes a long time to understand vegetables, cooking, and giving and receiving nourishing food. But what if that is only one half of the truth, one way of looking at things? What if it also takes no time at all, and we can understand everything right this moment? “Appreciate this carrot, cabbage, cucumber, and cress, this time with the less than perfect,” Brown reminds us. “The remarkable flavor you have searched for is everywhere. Let it come home to your heart.” Bon appétit!

Can Babies Learn to Love Vegetables? (Burkhard Bilger, The New Yorker, November 2019)

Every Halloween, Linus sits in the “most sincere” pumpkin patch with a signboard, awaiting the arrival of The Great Pumpkin. Will he come this year? Watch the 1966 classic “It’s the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown” on Apple TV. 

I’ve always been a vegetarian. You might think that would make me biased toward vegetables, and you’d be right. But when I was little, I routinely fantasized about installing a zipper in my belly so I could just shove the little devils in without ever taking my eyes off my comics. I eventually grew to love them, but could something have been done to smooth the way earlier?

The title question must be asked, for that’s where the story begins—babies and their smushed-up veggies. Bilger seeks an answer.

The enemy in question is kale. The four cups are all filled with raw kale leaves whipped into a smooth purée, or slurry, as food researchers call it. One sample is plain, another sweet, another sweeter still, and the last one salted. Sugar and salt can mask the bitterness in kale, but this baby isn’t fooled. No matter which sample he’s offered, he grimaces and turns his head, purses his lips, and swats the spoon away. The more his mother tries, the grumpier he gets, till he kicks his foot so hard that he jostles the electrode, disrupting the signal.

Stalking the Vegetannual (Barbara Kingsolver, Orion, March/April 2007)

Way before the Potato of Immaculate Conception, in the Middle Ages, there was the Vegetable Lamb of Tartary—“a strange hybrid creature, half-animal, half-plant.” Thom Sliwowski investigates old vegetable fancies for The Public Domain Review in “Animal, Vegetable, Lamb: The Zoophyte from Tartary.”

“Wait a minute,” a friend asks Kingsolver, “When you say, ‘the potatoes are up,’ what do you mean?” An urban, gourmet chef, she tries to puzzle it out some more: “What part of a potato comes up?” I find it somewhat hard to believe that a chef might not know the potato has a plant part, but who knows with us modern humans? We buy the vegetables that look appealing (and feel affordable) at the shop, never mind the season or the provenance.

Kingsolver has a remedy. She gives us “a roadmap to eating with the seasons”—a beautiful visual mnemonic, if you will, one you’re unlikely to forget once you’ve successfully pictured it. What’s better, it’s actually useful.

To recover an intuitive sense of what will be in season throughout the year, picture an imaginary plant that bears over the course of one growing season all the different vegetable products we can harvest. We’ll call it a vegetannual. Picture its life passing before your eyes like a time-lapse film: first, in the cool early spring, shoots poke up out of the ground. Small leaves appear, then bigger leaves. As the plant grows up into the sunshine and the days grow longer, flower buds will appear, followed by small green fruits. Under midsummer’s warm sun, the fruits grow larger, riper, and more colorful. As days shorten into the autumn, these mature into hard-shelled fruits with appreciable seeds inside. Finally, as the days grow cool, the vegetannual may hoard the sugars its leaves have made, pulling them down into a storage unit of some kind: a tuber, bulb, or root.

Plainly, all the vegetables we consume don’t come from the same plant, but each comes from a plant, that’s the point—a plant predestined to begin its life in the spring and die in the fall. (A few, like onions and carrots, are attempting to be biennials but we’ll ignore that for now.) What we choose to eat from each type of vegetable plant must come in its turn—leaves, buds, flowers, green fruits, ripe fruits, hard fruits—because that is the necessary order of things for an annual plant. For the life of them, they can’t do it differently.

Corn Tastes Better on the Honor System (Robin Wall Kimmerer, Emergence, October 2018)

“The corn provides a leafy ladder for the bean to climb, gaining access to more light and pollinators. In return, the bean fixes nitrogen, which feeds the demanding corn. The squash with its big leaves shades the soil, keeping it cool and moist while also suppressing weeds.” Read about this innovative polyculture in The Three Sisters chapter in Kimmerer’s Braiding Sweetgrass.

“The Seed of Seeds, Our Daily Bread, Wife of the Sun, and Mother of All Things.” “Mandamin, The Wonderful Seed.” “Mahiz, Bringer of Life.” I thought of the names this essay had given me for maize as I steamed some sweet corn this morning. In my culture, we ascribe this sacred role to rice; we never waste a grain of it. We’re losing this connection, though. Things are expensive now and real relationships—with land, with nature, with each other—cheap.

Contrasting indigenous maize cultivation perfected over 9,000 years in honor and reciprocity against industrial, GMO-driven monoculture, Kimmerer holds out hope—and method—for a positive way forward. A thing that stands out in Kimmerer’s writing is how much attention she pays to language—the language related to her subject matter as well as the language she uses to tell its story.

I hold in my hand four seeds in the colors of the medicine wheel: thundercloud black, solar yellow, pearly moonlight, and blood red. I hold in my hand the memory of my ancestors in the garden. The DNA in every cell carries the story of brown fingers poking these seeds into the earth, fingers just like mine, with dirt under their nails. These farmers nurtured not only food but extraordinary genetic diversity, with the capacity to adapt to changing climates and an always uncertain future. I could use some of that now. This is the fruit of sophisticated indigenous science: traditional ecological knowledge, known as TEK. The DNA beneath the shiny seed coat is the source of resourcefulness, the creativity of corn married to the nurture of the human. I hold in my hand the multicolored fruit of collective genius, an agreement between sun, soil, water, plant, and farmer. They have entered into a covenant of reciprocity: if the maize will take care of the people, the people will care for the maize.

How the Potato Changed the World (Charles C. Mann, Smithsonian, November 2011)

“[S]o often it comes down to one person who kept something small but important from being lost forever.” Here’s “History, Discovery, and the Quiet Heroics of Gardening” by Ursula Vernon for Reactor.

I love root vegetables (except that time when I found a bizarre thing in my farm box and shut the box real quick before googling to find out the thing was a celeriac). We have so many local ones here, each one earthier and nuttier than the other, but the potato still holds a special place.

Mann, a journalist, charts the colorful path of the humble potato through the world—from its birth in the Andes, its toxic Incan infancy, its voyage from the Americas to Europe in the holds of Spanish explorers, its starring role in famines and in industrial monoculture, all the way to its place in the world today.

Today the potato is the fifth most important crop worldwide, after wheat, corn, rice and sugar cane. But in the 18th century the tuber was a startling novelty, frightening to some, bewildering to others—part of a global ecological convulsion set off by Christopher Columbus.

About 250 million years ago, the world consisted of a single giant landmass now known as Pangaea. Geological forces broke Pangaea apart, creating the continents and hemispheres familiar today. Over the eons, the separate corners of the earth developed wildly different suites of plants and animals. Columbus’s voyages reknit the seams of Pangaea, to borrow a phrase from Alfred W. Crosby, the historian who first described this process. In what Crosby called the Columbian Exchange, the world’s long-separate ecosystems abruptly collided and mixed in a biological bedlam that underlies much of the history we learn in school. The potato flower in Louis XVI’s buttonhole, a species that had crossed the Atlantic from Peru, was both an emblem of the Columbian Exchange and one of its most important aspects.

A Brief History of Onions in America (Mark Kurlansky, Literary Hub, November 2023)

The poet Pablo Neruda wrote 225 odes to all manner of things, most of them ordinary. Here’s “Oda a la cebolla,” or, “Ode to the Onion.”

You wouldn’t know it to look at the onion now, sitting quietly in a sack in the corner, but it had a checkered past, crisscrossing the world and shaking things up. Onions for the Maya; onions for the Aztecs; onions for Mexicans, Native Americans, and Europeans. Onions for conquerors and colonists, explorers and naturalists, kings and presidents, and for people just going about their daily cooking. Everyone had to have their bit of alliaceous magic, and the onion put down roots for good.

This essay, excerpted from Kurlansky’s award-winning book, The Core of an Onion: Peeling the Rarest Common Food (featuring old photographs, hand-drawn illustrations, and a hundred historical recipes), traces the onion’s redolent route through America.

Elizabeth Bacon Custer, the widow of the infamous George Armstrong Custer, did not write of his racism and genocide, but she did write about onions while camping in the west with Custer, saying that they were “as rare out there, and more appreciated than pomegranates are in New York.”

Custer and his younger brother Tom, who also died on the Little Bighorn, were zealous cepaphiles. But apparently, in a rare criticism, Elizabeth was not fond of her husband’s onion breath. In an 1873 letter to his wife while on an expedition to the Yellowstone River, Custer wrote that he was filling up on onions now that he was away from her. “I supped on RAW ONIONS; I will probably breakfast, lunch and dine on them tomorrow, and the next day, and the day after ad libitum ad infinitum . . . . Go it old fellow! Make the most of your liberties! . . . . If you intend to eat raw onions now is your only time for ‘missus is comin.’ ”

Politics of the Plate: The Price of Tomatoes (Barry Estabrook, Gourmet (Archived), March 2009)

“In 1893, nine men, collectively known as the Justices of the US Supreme Court, had to decide whether the tomato is legally a fruit or a vegetable.” Spoiler: “It’s a Vegetable, Goddamn It!”

If you think the biggest trouble with the tomato is figuring out whether it’s a fruit or a vegetable, this James Beard Award-winning essay by investigative food journalist Estabrook will quickly disabuse you of the notion. This essay seeded his New York Times-bestselling exposé Tomatoland, revised and republished a few years ago with a ton of updated material. 

What exactly is the human and environmental cost of the beautiful red tomato that we love? Can things change for the better, not just for a few but for everyone?

Driving from Naples, Florida, the nation’s second-wealthiest metropolitan area, to Immokalee takes less than an hour on a straight road. You pass houses that sell for an average of $1.4 million, shopping malls anchored by Tiffany’s and Saks Fifth Avenue, manicured golf courses. Eventually, gated communities with names like Monaco Beach Club and Imperial Golf Estates give way to modest ranches, and the highway shrivels from six lanes to two. Through the scruffy palmettos, you glimpse flat, sandy tomato fields shimmering in the broiling sun. Rounding a long curve, you enter Immokalee. The heart of town is a nine-block grid of dusty, potholed streets lined by boarded-up bars and bodegas, peeling shacks, and sagging, mildew-streaked house trailers. Mongrel dogs snooze in the shade, scrawny chickens peck in yards. Just off the main drag, vultures squabble over roadkill. Immokalee’s population is 70 percent Latino. Per capita income is only $8,500 a year. One third of the families in this city of nearly 25,000 live below the poverty line. Over one third of the children drop out before graduating from high school.

Immokalee is the tomato capital of the United States. Between December and May, as much as 90 percent of the fresh domestic tomatoes we eat come from south Florida, and Immokalee is home to one of the area’s largest communities of farmworkers. According to Douglas Molloy, the chief assistant U.S. attorney based in Fort Myers, Immokalee has another claim to fame: It is “ground zero for modern slavery.”

Japan’s Ancient Vegetarian Meal (Lily Crossley-Baxter, BBC, September 2020)

In the two-episode Netflix miniseries “The Philosopher’s Kitchen Jeong Kwan,” Korean Buddhist nun and chef Jeong Kwan works with nature and the seasons, gathering local vegetables, wild greens, and gentle seasonings to cook wonderful, nourishing temple food. 

Dōgen, a thirteenth-century monk who founded the Sōtō school of Zen in Japan, wrote many philosophical and poetic works. He also wrote a tiny manual called Tenzo Kyōkun, or Instructions for the Cook. For some 800 years, this text—along with traditions like the sixth-century shōjin ryōri, “food for spiritual practice,” that adopted its ideas—has guided Buddhist temple cooking according to certain spiritual and philosophical principles. 

This method uses seasonal, nutritious plants and mindful techniques of cooking, serving, and eating to achieve balance and harmony for body, mind, and spirit, as Crossley-Baxter experiences firsthand.

Edged in vibrant pink, a shadow-thin slice of radish sits atop a soft square of sesame tofu. Beside it, a pot of udon simmers gently while a nearby basket holds a nest of crisp tempura—forming just three of the dozen dishes set before me. We are seated in a quiet tatami room at Ekoin, one of more than 100 temples that form the ancient complex of Koya in rural Wakayama prefecture. Perched on the mountainside, the town is the centre of Shingon Buddhism, and our meal is known as shōjin ryōri, a spiritual cuisine perfected by monks over centuries.

Known for its moss-covered cemeteries and forested pilgrimage routes, Koya is home to a long tradition of worship. The town’s many temple lodgings, known as shukubo, offer visitors the chance to experience the ways of Buddhism, from meditation to calligraphy—but few know that the humble temple meals are also an opportunity for spiritual exploration.

IT’S DECORATIVE GOURD SEASON, MOTHERFUCKERS

“I don’t know about you, but I can’t wait to get my hands on some fucking gourds and arrange them in a horn-shaped basket on my dining room table. That shit is going to look so seasonal.”

Every autumn, Colin Nissan’s “freaky-ass harvest” classic for McSweeney’s, their “most-read article of all time,” makes a comeback. You see why.

Kanya Kanchana is a writer from India.

Editor: Krista Stevens

Copyeditor: Brendan Fitzgerald

entries.title: “The River Can’t Be Trusted”
entries.summary: "On July 8, 2025, three people at an RV park died in a flood. Some first responders say the tragedy could have been avoided, while leaders insist they did all they could."
entries.content:
Last year, a powerful flood swept through the small village of Ruidoso, New Mexico, devastating the popular Ruidiso Downs race track and Riverview RV Park. Local responders warned people around the track, which one reporter called “a major driver for the mountain village’s economy.” No such warnings reached the RV park, which fell within the village’s floodplain and where, ultimately, three campers were killed. As post-fire floods present a growing challenge throughout the American West, Abe Streep’s investigative feature for ProPublica offers a riveting look at the disturbing questions that haunt survivors in the aftermath.

The water kept coming, fanning onto roads until the normal course of the river disappeared. What the wall of brown water carried told residents it was time to panic.

Jason Fulcher, an owner of the Riverview RV Park, saw a tree-size log in the waterway. Two miles downstream, a maintenance worker at a mobile home park saw a car float past and lodge against a bridge.

Farther downstream, the track’s executives did not need physical signs of danger; they knew what was coming because they’d been alerted.

But the Trotters were caught unprepared. Around 3 p.m., they retreated to their trailer to escape the rain. Then the flood tore through a wall and took their children.

More stories from the aftermath of disaster

What if America Went Completely Dark?

“The power grid relies on thousands of aging, hand-built transformers. If enough fail, the blackout could last years.”

Could the Girls of Camp Mystic Have Been Saved?

“Dozens died in a Texas flood, dividing families over whether it was an act of God or adult failure.”

Racing’s Deadliest Day

“How the 1955 Le Mans disaster changed motorsport forever.”

entries.title: The Secret Life of the NBA’s Most Mysterious Blogger
entries.summary: "For decades, Bob Windrem has obsessively chronicled the Brooklyn Nets under a pseudonym. But the man behind NetsDaily has spent much of his life chasing secrets—and keeping a few of his own."
entries.content:
Eighty-one-year-old Bob Windrem spent half his life at NBC News. As a senior investigative producer, he drew on CIA sources to feed Tom Brokaw early info on the September 11 terrorist attacks. He filed stories about the Chernobyl nuclear disaster and cartel violence in Mexico, and went undercover in Johannesburg to help reveal Israel’s role in South Africa’s missile development program. Today, he’s perhaps best known as “Net Income,” the name under which he’s chronicled the Brooklyn Nets for more than two decades. James Herbert’s profile is an entertaining look at the journalistic chops of an octogenarian NBA blogger who kept his hard-news edge, and the most interesting guy lurking just outside the locker room.

Before he’d written a word for NetsDaily, Windrem was the main character on the NJ.com forum. Many posters hated how he defended the front office’s decision to let Kenyon Martin walk in 2004. The personal attacks he receives now can be a bit much, but Windrem either throws a jab back or rolls his eyes. “I’m a big boy. I’ve been yelled at by members of the Iranian Revolutionary Guard and the White House press secretary and TV anchors,” he said. He can handle a few mean tweets.

A few basketball stories where the drama is off the court

The Anatomy of a Journalism Scandal

“The first time ‘The New York Times’ had lost a defamation case in over half a century.”

Online Trolls Harassed Her Six-Year-Old. That Was Only the Beginning.

“How a group of sports fans at the University of Iowa sparked a clash involving a basketball star, a T-shirt company, and a reporter from halfway across the country.”

Inside the Shaolin Monastery that Helped Build Victor Wembanyama

“This is the story of how 34 generations of Shaolin warrior history trained a once-in-a-generation NBA superstar.”

entries.title: The Influencers’ Influencer
entries.summary: MFK Fisher’s clandestine campaign to spread Japanese cuisine and transform American food culture
entries.content:
This essay is co-published with Vittles and appears in Vittles Issue No. 3: The Influencers.

Vaughn Tan | Longreads | November 24, 2026 | 3,989 words (17 minutes)

Back in 2003, I was in the early stages of researching how the distinctive visual style of Japanese plating and dish design influenced plating outside Japan, and wanted to analyze photos of fine-dining dishes in industry periodicals like Art Culinaire. Back in the early 2000s, this was easiest to do in libraries. At the time, I lived in Cambridge, Massachusetts, so I wound up in the collection of historical cookbooks and culinary materials at the Schlesinger Library.

One afternoon, Barbara Haber, then the Schlesinger’s curator of books, stopped by my desk with something for me: Japanese Cooking: A Simple Art by Shizuo Tsuji, published in 1980 with an introduction by MFK Fisher. I knew of Fisher through her essays on eating and her translation of Brillat-Savarin’s The Physiology of Taste, but not for anything related to Japanese food. Barbara mentioned that many boxes of Fisher’s collected papers had recently arrived at the library. The papers were still uncatalogued, but was I interested in looking at them?

I didn’t know then that I was beginning a 20-year detour. As I went through these boxes over the next few months, my original research project faded away. I found myself more and more drawn to the Fisher archive boxes, and to the story that emerged as I read through years of her correspondence and other documents, including letters about her trip to Japan to research the introduction she wrote to Japanese Cooking; letters about the book she wrote to journalists, writers, and editors across the US; and draft manuscripts of Japanese Cooking, with her comments in red pen, which had crisscrossed the Pacific between California and Osaka. The story that emerged was of a secret campaign Fisher waged between 1979 and 1982, which was instrumental in the seemingly sudden transformation of Japanese food into fine dining in America.

Fisher’s campaign worked well because it was largely invisible. The publishers of Japanese Cooking didn’t know that any of this was happening. Ruth Reichl, who wrote the foreword to the 25th anniversary edition in 2005, had no idea Fisher had done any more than write the introduction when I spoke to her earlier this year. (Fisher had gifted her a copy of the book before Reichl’s first trip to Japan in the early 1980s.) Yet Fisher not only shaped the book itself, she also systematically put it in front of everyone who mattered in the American food world—people whose endorsement could not be bought, and whose reasons for endorsing the book were, as I later realized, largely Fisher’s own.

In 2003, I wasn’t sure what to do with my discovery. It didn’t fit any story I knew how to tell yet. And although it made sense to me back then that no one had uncovered this evidence before—Fisher’s campaign was visible only through forensic analysis of an uncatalogued archive, and left no traces in the places people normally look—in the years since, it has remained largely unexamined, even though Fisher is an extensively examined writer. Her reputation has grown considerably over the past two decades and, in the UK especially, she is now frequently invoked as the great American food writer.

But the Fisher I uncovered in those boxes was someone else, and her role in making Japanese food into fine dining in America remains almost entirely unknown. This is what she did.

To properly understand Fisher’s impact, we must first understand how quickly the perception of Japanese food changed in the US. It happened in just a few years.

For many decades, French cuisine was the only one perceived as legitimate fine dining in the US. Japanese cuisine didn’t come close to meeting that standard. Until the late 1970s, Japanese food wasn’t just exotic to the American public, it was fundamentally alien. Craig Claiborne, the influential food editor of the New York Times, posed a seemingly genuine rhetorical question in the paper in 1974: “Who can persuade John Doe that there is much to be said in a positive sense for cooked chrysanthemum leaves … and pickled petals of the chrysanthemum flower?” And it wasn’t just John Doe who had to be convinced; the culinary elite didn’t understand Japanese food either. Kim Schuefftan, formerly of Kodansha International (which published Japanese Cooking), told me about meeting an American food writer in the 1970s who complained that the broth in hiyayakko (a dish of chilled and garnished delicate tofu) was “under-flavoured.” (Schuefftan’s reaction: “Of course it’s under-flavoured, you stupid idiot, it’s water!”)

The usual explanation of how the perception of Japanese food changed in the US runs like this: Japan’s economy grew through the 1970s into one of the world’s largest, so Japanese corporations planted roots in American cities and Japanese executives arrived who wanted to eat Japanese food. Meanwhile, the Magnuson-Stevens Act of 1976 expanded American fishing zones, meaning that sushi-grade fish began to appear in the US (and Americans gradually started to eat sushi). Although Japan’s growing economic power was part of the story, it couldn’t automatically generate cultural prestige overseas and cannot alone explain why Japanese cooking was suddenly valued by the same cultural elite who had been ignoring it for years.

For Japanese cuisine to be genuinely appreciated as fine dining in America, it had to be translated, its logic made intelligible to people who didn’t grow up with it—as Madhur Jaffrey had done for Indian cooking, or as Fuchsia Dunlop would go on to do for Sichuan cooking. And for that translation to move fast through a cultural milieu requires a sponsor, someone willing to put their reputation behind the idea—to write the letters, call in the favours and spend their credibility to get the people they trusted to take the new thing seriously. MFK Fisher was that person, through the channel of Japanese Cooking.

Then, as now, the legible way influence manifests is via public figures with large platforms who tell the public what to think. But upstream of those visible tastemakers are often unknown people who shape these tastemakers’ taste, éminences grises whom Mimi Sheraton (the former New York Times food critic) describes as “the people who go out and find new things and decide what they like for themselves, people who actually have taste . . . When I find them, I usually listen to them.” While the idea of Japanese food as worthy of consideration might have reached the masses through Claiborne, or through restaurant critics like Sheraton, or through Julia Child on television, Fisher was where the idea originated.

Fisher was a highly respected writer. WH Auden wrote that he didn’t know of anyone in the United States who wrote better prose, and she had a prized New Yorker writer’s agreement shared only with legendary writers like Susan Sontag, EB White, and John McPhee. But she wasn’t a mass-media presence; she lived outside the cultural metropolises—in Sonoma County, a rural winemaking part of California. Nonetheless, the cultural elite came to visit. James Beard, who championed a distinct American culinary identity, made the journey. So did Craig Claiborne, Alice Waters, Mimi Sheraton, Ruth Reichl, and many others. Mary Sutherland, who worked closely with Fisher and would later play a central role in the Tsuji book, described Fisher’s situation: “Mary Frances, especially before the Food Network and that sort of thing, was the royalty of the food world, and all her pals were the other royalty too.”

Shizuo Tsuji made the journey as well. In 1962, he wrote to Fisher asking for introductions to the French culinary scene after reading her translation of The Physiology of Taste. Just two years previously, Tsuji had founded his cooking school in Osaka, which would go on to become Japan’s largest culinary academy, and he had ambitions that extended beyond Japan. Fisher connected him to Simone Beck (one of Child’s co-authors on Mastering the Art of French Cooking), to Paul Bocuse and Alain Senderens (architects of nouvelle cuisine), and to Fernand Point (who had trained a generation of France’s greatest chefs at La Pyramide in Vienne). Tsuji’s son, Yoshiki, who now runs the Tsuji Culinary Institute in Osaka, later told me that his father and Fisher shared “fine humour in pessimism”: They saw clearly what was wrong with the world, and could laugh about it.

This was the foundation of a decades-long correspondence. Tsuji sent Fisher translations of teaching materials about Japanese cooking he had prepared for his Osaka cooking school. Though Fisher doesn’t seem to have had any previous interest in Japanese food before her correspondence with him, by 1974, she had become convinced that Tsuji was uniquely qualified to introduce Japanese food to America. She had grown increasingly disgusted with what American food was becoming (“greasy Kentucky Fried Chicken, airflown plastic fruit,” and cooking increasingly stripped of attention and care), and the Japanese approach to cooking taught at Tsuji’s school seemed to represent the alternative she sought.

A book, she thought, would be the perfect medium to introduce this culinary philosophy to America. That same year, Fisher wrote to Tsuji with a suggestion for how to approach the book: he should “assume that [he is] trying to explain to a group of American cooks the differences between their techniques and those in Japan.” This idea became the conceptual foundation of Japanese Cooking: A Simple Art, a book that wouldn’t come into existence for another six years. And it was Fisher’s agreeing in 1978 to write the introduction that finally convinced Tsuji that the book could succeed and so should be written.

As part of writing the introduction, Tsuji invited Fisher and her sister Norah Barr to Japan to experience “only the very best of the Japanese Cuisine with its profound and abundant culture.” The trip was, according to Schuefftan, “carefully and rigorously circumscribed”: Tsuji was determined to show Fisher a great time. Their schedule included lessons in Japanese cooking from Tsuji’s most experienced culinary instructors and visits to the country’s top restaurants (many of which served kaiseki, multi-course menus that instantiate the technical and referential sophistication of Japanese cooking). They ate at Kitcho—a fabled Kyoto kaiseki restaurant at which a trusted patron’s introduction was needed to get a reservation—three times in two weeks. (Schuefftan: “It was unheard of.”) Tsuji’s protégé Koichiro Hata, who did the cooking demonstrations for Fisher, remembered thinking that “Tsuji spared no expense . . . he respected her very much, so he tried his hardest to make her feel good and welcomed.” Sutherland, who was involved in preparations for the trip, confirmed that “Tsuji completely controlled exactly what they saw and what they did.”

For her part, Fisher wasn’t entirely reverent about the experience. Writing to her friend, landlord and benefactor, David Pleydell-Bouverie, she describes an evening at a restaurant spent “wondering how in hell to arise gracefully after fourteen courses of exquisite nothings,” where, as “ladies,” she and Norah “were served only two sips of sake, and the rest was tea,” with “the great Anglo-Saxon oxes with their long legs dying . . . Murder.” She was “incredulous at prices.” (Kitcho would have been one of the most expensive restaurants in Japan.) She called herself “the Daisy Miller of Nippon cuisine”—a naive American abroad, in over her head. Yet, when she returned to America, she found herself a convert to Japanese cooking. She wrote to her sister about “cultural withdrawal” and a sudden distaste for butter, salt, cream. She wrote to Child:

If I could eat the unprocurable things that Tsuji managed to present to us as lessons in what present Japanese cooking is based on, I would gladly eat nothing else for the rest of my life. I would forgo every subtle dish I have ever tasted in the past seventy years. This is a shattering statement to make, and of course there is no risk of its ever happening, but it is true.

Fisher was more convinced than ever that she’d found the corrective she believed American eating needed. Tsuji, meanwhile, wanted Japanese Cooking to serve as “a cultural embassy to America.” As Sutherland explained to me, Tsuji believed there were “three main cuisines: French, Chinese, and Japanese.” He wanted Japanese food to “take its rightful place in the pantheon,” and Fisher was the instrument of transmission who could enable him to achieve this goal.

Tsuji paid Fisher only to write an introduction to his book. But her archive shows how her ideas shaped the entire project. At Fisher’s insistence, Part One of Japanese Cooking, which comprises 300 of the book’s 518 pages, is a treatise on Japanese cooking written for Americans, covering everything from the structure of a meal to the logic of Japanese ingredients, to important foundational cooking techniques. She was convinced that Japanese cooking could only become comprehensible to American readers and cooks if they had rich context about this fundamentally different approach to cuisine.

The technique lessons drew directly from Koichiro Hata’s demonstrations for Fisher in Osaka, the structuring of the content presented closely matched to the questions she was asking during those lessons. Today, many cookbooks begin with a similar prefatory section, but at the time it was not common practice. Fisher also provided feedback on successive drafts of the manuscript, rewriting it to make unfamiliar ideas more legible and flagging recipes whose ingredients were unobtainable in America or that were simply too difficult. (She wrote “An impossible recipe!” next to a recipe for deep-fried “sesame-ship” sole.) She insisted that recipes be illustrated with line drawings, not photographs, over the protests of Kodansha’s senior art staff: she knew photographs would date, whereas drawings would not. (The book is still in print, and fundamentally unrevised, more than four decades later.) She insisted on having a researcher in San Francisco compile a robust list of American ingredient substitutions: “There’s really no use printing a fine traditional recipe simply because of its historical or esthetic [sic] value, if the western reader cannot even try to duplicate it.” And she gave the book its subtitle, A Simple Art, though as Schuefftan said, “The amount of effort which goes into making something appear simple is simply awesome.”

Japanese Cooking was released in November 1980. The first printing of 15,000 copies sold out before the official release, and over 65,000 copies sold in the first four months. These were great sales numbers for any kind of cookbook, and almost unimaginable at the time for a book focused on a non-Western cuisine. Almost 40% of orders came from professional culinary institutions, suggesting that restaurant owners and chefs were reading the book “for ideas on how to use ingredients differently, ideas on new flavours and combinations of flavours, ideas on food presentation,” according to Sutherland. The book’s unexpected success at launch was largely due to a spate of articles about it in major newspapers and food publications. In December 1980, Fisher wrote to Tsuji, “I don’t think that any book about the Japanese cuisine has ever had such ‘press.'”

What she doesn’t mention in the letter is how strongly she shaped the book’s reception. Her correspondence with editors and writers in San Francisco, Chicago, Boston, Los Angeles and Washington DC between 1979 and 1981 reveals a precisely targeted promotional campaign, one in which Kodansha was not involved. (Its publicity department was, Sutherland recalled, “very, very weak.”) Fisher had been laying the groundwork for this well before the book even existed. As far back as 1963, she had encouraged Rachel MacKenzie, a New Yorker editor, to have the magazine interview Tsuji during a New York visit. The magazine finally ran a 1978 profile of Tsuji by John Bainbridge titled “A Worried Man” after Fisher suggested it in a letter she wrote to the editor, William Shawn.

As Japanese Cooking neared publication, Fisher proposed a second New Yorker piece on Tsuji: an excerpt of her introduction to his book. Shawn declined with regret; the magazine’s policy prohibited two features on the same topic. What happened next showed Fisher’s network operating at speed. The morning after the New Yorker passed, Fisher got a call from her agent. He had spoken to an editor at the magazine Food & Wine who wanted to publish the piece. Less than 24 hours from rejection to placement, and not by coincidence. Fisher had separately written to Ariane and Michael Batterberry, Food & Wine’s editors and her personal friends, asking them to run the piece. Alongside a section from Fisher’s introduction, Food & Wine’s chefs, who were “completely ignorant of Japanese techniques,” tested recipes from Japanese Cooking and were “amazed by the basic simplicity and the success of what they did.” The piece was titled “MFK Fisher and the Art of Japanese Cooking.” Her name was the draw, as the editors’ note on the article made explicit: “No one could be a more astute and sensitive observer of shifting gastronomic patterns, waning culinary traditions, and the rising and ebbing quality of food and drink than MFK Fisher.” And, as Sutherland had told Fisher months earlier, the staff at Food & Wine “know the dollar value of your work, your name, and the loyal audience you have.”

When I told Schuefftan about Fisher’s various efforts to make tastemakers promote the book, he was shocked: “You’re kidding!” When I told him she’d also arranged the New Yorker profile from which the book had benefitted two years earlier he was equally surprised. “I had no idea she did that. We never asked her.” From 1979 to 1981, Fisher’s correspondence with food writers and reviewers about Japanese Cooking was carefully tailored to each recipient. She considered who had been to Japan, who had written about Asian food previously, who might be reached better through mutual friends rather than directly. Her campaign was meticulous and patient, built over years rather than launched in weeks. Claiborne (who, as food editor of the New York Times, had an enormous impact on what American restaurant goers thought they should eat) was Fisher’s close friend. Sutherland witnessed the effect Fisher had on Claiborne’s view of Japanese Cooking directly: “Mary Frances told Craig Claiborne about it. And when I met him, it was clear that he’d read it very thoroughly, and he was recommending it to everybody.” Fisher’s recommendation produced three glowing articles and reviews in the New York Times in 1980 and 1981. When the paper asked prominent chefs what they wanted for Christmas in 1980, Beck and Child both said Japanese Cooking.

And more reviews followed in other publications. Judith Huxley, reviewing the book in the Washington Post in January 1981, wrote that serious engagement with Japanese cooking in the West had been nearly impossible for want of a serious English-language guide, a “void” that was “filled by the recent publication of Japanese Cooking.” In April 1981, Japanese Cooking became a “Book of the Month Club” selection, “because of the interest from the professional cooking circles,” Sutherland explained. For a small publisher like Kodansha, this was an astonishing result. The Book of the Month Club had over a million subscribers at the time: predominantly the educated middle class, who formed the core of the serious home-cooking audience. It offered a guaranteed readership of tens of thousands of people already predisposed to take it seriously.

Notably, except for a small fee she received from Food & Wine for the reprinting of her introduction, Fisher’s efforts to promote Japanese Cooking do not seem to have brought her any additional financial reward. She didn’t receive royalties from book sales. Perhaps this seeming impartiality is why the culinary elite trusted her endorsement: they knew that it wasn’t being bought.

While it’s impossible to quantify just how central Fisher’s efforts were to Japanese Cooking’s critical and commercial success, another carefully produced book about Japanese food for an American audience published contemporaneously is a useful comparator. In 1980, Knopf published At Home with Japanese Cooking by Elizabeth Andoh, an American writer living in Japan. Andoh’s book had strong editorial credentials: It was edited by Judith Jones, who had also worked with Julia Child, Marcella Hazan and Madhur Jaffrey. Nonetheless, it sold far fewer copies than Tsuji’s Japanese Cooking. A book about the same cuisine, at the same moment, for the same market, and released by a major American publisher, but without Fisher’s invisible hand to move the needle.

In 1982, historian Sallie Williams wrote that Japanese cuisine was “perhaps the greatest growing influence on food presentation in America today.” Barbara Haber, the Schlesinger curator who built the institute’s culinary book collection, credits Japanese Cooking with being “the book that any chef worth his salt will tell you made Japanese food big in America.” Japanese cuisine has remained in the first rank of world cuisines ever since, the only non-Western cuisine widely regarded to be at the same level as French. In New York and Los Angeles, the most expensive, hardest-to-book restaurants are now more likely to be omakase counters than a temple of French cuisine.

Although Fisher died in 1992 (Tsuji died a year later), the cuisine she spent decades quietly promoting still occupies the position she believed it deserved. The version of Japanese cuisine that crossed the Pacific was filtered twice—first through Tsuji’s careful management of Fisher’s visit to Japan, and then by Fisher’s American interpretation of what she experienced. As such, it was a highly selective view of the cuisine, representing what Tsuji wanted an American food writer to experience and report back on. To win that legibility, much of the breadth and variety of Japanese cooking was lost.

More broadly, the embrace of Japanese Cooking didn’t transform American food culture in the way Fisher hoped it would. As Reichl said when I spoke to her, “What Mary Frances hoped for hasn’t come to pass . . . We have not taken any of the good lessons from Japanese cuisine.” Fisher had wanted Japanese Cooking to teach Americans restraint, precision, and deep attention to ingredients. The message about Japanese cooking that eventually made it through was that raw fish is acceptable at a business lunch.

But in today’s ambitious restaurants, there is now an emphasis on seasonal and local ingredients, and a strong attachment to the notion that simplicity can be a form of mastery. These ideas spread through the American fine-dining establishment in the 1980s and 1990s after Japanese Cooking was published. Fisher and Tsuji’s names aren’t explicitly attached to these changes, in keeping with the invisible ways in which she operated.

In the years since I uncovered this history in 2003, I have tried several times to interest agents and publishers in it. The feedback, each time, was the same: The story wasn’t of wide enough interest. There was also a tacit resistance to a story whose protagonist is a white literary establishment woman mediating, behind the scenes, the introduction of a non-Western cuisine to America. That’s not how the food world has wanted to see itself in recent years.

But the hidden story of Japanese Cooking is just another story of influence over ideas: who wields it, how it works, and how it persists, even without our realizing. Reichl absorbed Fisher’s ideas before she had a platform to say so. Claiborne, Beard and Child before her were shaped by Fisher too. Even Schuefftan—who worked on Japanese Cooking through its entire gestation, who thought its success was due to Tsuji’s charisma—operated inside a world Fisher had covertly arranged.

This is how influence works: It moves through people who pass it on without attribution, not because they are dishonest, but because it is part of the cultural air they breathe. Though it may seem that only the impact we can see is important, the archive says otherwise. Maybe it will emerge that, behind every major food writer, chef or critic with a following in 2026, there was someone like Fisher secretly shaping their landscape of taste. We may find out in 20 years, when someone else goes looking.

Vaughn Tan is the executive director of Tangent, an AI-informed incubator in Singapore. Previously, he was founding faculty at University College London’s School of Management, and worked at Google in California. His personal website is here. You can also find him on X and Instagram.

entries.title: ‘Ask For What You Want’ Is a Key Skill For the 21st Century
entries.summary: "Seeing a new icon in your dock drives home the understanding: this environment is malleable. It can, at last, be anything I want."
entries.content:
On his blog, author Robin Sloan shares observations on working with AI agents to build a native desktop app. He’s cautious and critical of AI, and explains his process to creative people who are wary of it. But, ultimately, he encourages experimentation.

Okay, so. With the help of the AI agent, you make your first app. It bounces merrily in the dock. I want to underscore, what’s important is not that it’s a notes app, or a sleek jukebox, or whatever. You can already get every kind of app. What’s important is that it’s yours. It’s weird and specific, and it won’t change unless you want it to change.

“I want to frame the technology more like an instrument, and get away from GenAI as an intelligence, an ideology, a tool, a crutch, or a weapon.”

entries.title: The Old and The Furious
entries.summary: "As Americans live longer than ever, car crashes involving elderly adults are on the rise. The question is what to do about it—and how many more deadly accidents it will take for us to act."
entries.content:
Americans are living longer these days, long enough to become vehicular terrors behind the wheel in their eighties and nineties, and they’re injuring themselves and others at unprecedented rates. David Howard, with additional reporting from Lloyd Alter, does the math and suggests that simply taking a senior’s licence away is not the answer; America is car-centric and many seniors need to drive in order to grocery shop, attend health appointments, and to meet their social needs. Could autonomous vehicles provide the balance we need between safety and independence?

Already visible on the technological horizon, of course, are self-driving cars, which carry the potential to obviate many of the limitations older drivers face. Mark Needham (not his real name) lives on the fringes of Charlottesville, Virgina. He is 82 and still active: He practices yoga at a local health club, engages in a glassblowing hobby, and dabbles with technology. He and his wife, 80, have lived in the same subdivision for 40 years, and while she’s wrestling with several health issues and is ready to move into a retirement facility, he’s adamantly opposed to it. “My wife is more inclined to being taken care of,” Needham says.

“I’m more inclined to be doing stuff.”

Part of what allows him to maintain his independence: a Tesla that over his two-plus years of ownership has morphed, via a steady stream of software updates, into a largely autonomous vehicle. (Many reviewers and experts still cite the need for improvement with tasks like changing speeds and parking before use becomes widespread.) “It drives better than I drove 30 or 40 years ago,” he says.

More picks on aging

No iPad Till After Dinner, Mom

“Seniors are spending more time than ever on their slop-filled feeds. It’s their adult children’s job to save them.”

The Seniors Against Senior Housing

“America’s elders need more places to live, but even in liberal enclaves that recognize the problem, developers are facing the fiercest foes of all: America’s elders.”

My Father Wants to Age in Place. AI Will Be Watching

“Devices that monitor seniors for safety are appealing to worried loved ones and underresourced home care agencies.”

entries.title: Juiced to the Gills
entries.content:
You have, by now, read something about the Enhanced Games, the steroid-fueled athletic spectacle held this year in Las Vegas. (Perhaps we even recommended it.) But there’s nothing quite like seeing the event through Kent Russell’s eyes as he sneaks high-proof whiskey from his ThermoFlask, considers the physical demands of parenting and his own life’s onrushing decline, and concedes that a drug-enhanced life sounds “pretty fucking dope.”

As of this moment, the sprinters are clean, the Erth bleachers are searing the backs of my thighs, and Michael Bryan is overawing me through the act of locomotion. I sip from my thermos and bask in wonderment that a human body can be made to move that way. Beauty of this kind, which eighteenth-century types correctly filed under the category of the sublime, requires that it exceed me. A thing I could do myself is admirable; a thing that no effort of mine could ever accomplish, that lives permanently past my ceiling, is awesome in the old, strong sense of the word, in which awe is part fear, part love, part recognition that I am small and soft. The unfairness is the source of the wonder. To resent that Bryan is gifted beyond me is to resent that the thing I’m watching is beautiful, which is insane and would require that I demand the world contain nothing larger than myself.
